1:
In Rājagaha, a rich merchant’s daughter became intimate with a servant. Fearing her parents’ punishment,
they took their valuables and left by the main gate for a distant land.
3:
She brought the boys to Rājagaha to show them their mother’s family, but her parents would not see her;
they sent money and asked only for the children. The boys grew up in their grandfather’s house.
4: The elder, Mahāpanthaka, was drawn to the Buddha’s teaching, went forth, and in time became an arahant.
5:
With their grandfather’s consent the elder had Cūḷapanthaka ordained too. But because he had once mocked a slow monk
in the time of Kassapa Buddha, after four months he still could not learn a single verse.
6: His elder brother, who was in charge of the meals, said, “You are unfit for this teaching. Leave here,” and sent him out of the monastery.
7:
When Jīvaka invited the monks to a meal, the elder brother accepted for all except his younger brother,
saying, “Cūḷapanthaka is dull and does not grow in the Dhamma.”
8:
Thinking his brother had turned against him, Cūḷapanthaka set out at dawn to return to lay life.
Knowing this, the Buddha went ahead and stopped him: “Your going forth depends on me.”
9: The Buddha gave him a clean piece of cloth made by psychic power, and told him to sit facing east, rubbing it and repeating, “Removal of impurity.”
10:
Seeing the clean cloth grow dirty as he rubbed it, he saw impermanence. The Buddha spoke verses: “The true dirt is greed, hatred and delusion,”
and at their end he became an arahant.
11:
At Jīvaka’s house the elder brother said, “No monks are left in the monastery.” The Buddha said, “There are.”
Jīvaka sent a man to find out.
12:
To show his brother was wrong, Cūḷapanthaka created a thousand monks by psychic power;
the messenger found the Mango Grove full of them.
13: He called, “Cūḷapanthaka!” and a thousand voices answered. When he took the first one by the hand, the others vanished.
14:
After the meal the Buddha told Jīvaka, “Take Cūḷapanthaka’s bowl; he will give the thanksgiving,”
and Cūḷapanthaka taught Jīvaka the Dhamma.
15:
That evening, as the monks praised the Buddha in the hall, he came and said,
“Through me Cūḷapanthaka has now gained the great Dhamma; in the past, great wealth.”
Then the monks asked him to tell that story.
16:
Long ago in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a treasurer called Cūḷaseṭṭhi. Seeing a dead mouse,
he said, “A sharp young man could support a wife and start a business with this.”
17: Trusting the treasurer’s words, a poor young man picked up the dead mouse.
18: He sold the mouse as food for a cat and received one kākaṇikā, the smallest coin.
19:
With the coin he bought molasses and a water-pot, and gave water and molasses to flower-gatherers coming from the forest.
They gave him flowers, and selling them he earned eight kahāpaṇas.
20:
A great storm filled the king’s garden with branches, and the gardener had no way to clear them.
When he offered to clear it all if he could keep the wood, the gardener gladly agreed.
21: He gave molasses to the children at play and had them pile the branches at the garden gate.
22:
The king’s potter, needing fuel to fire pots for the palace, bought the firewood for sixteen kahāpaṇas and five vessels.
Now he had twenty-four kahāpaṇas.
23: At the city gate he gave water to five hundred grass-cutters, and they promised to help him.
24:
A land-route friend told him a horse-dealer would come tomorrow with five hundred horses,
so he asked the grass-cutters to bring him a bundle each and not to sell grass to the dealer.
25:
Finding no fodder anywhere in the city,
the horse-dealer bought his five hundred bundles of grass for a thousand kahāpaṇas.
26:
A few days later a friend who worked the water routes
told him that a great ship had come into port.
27:
He hired a carriage for eight kahāpaṇas, went to the port in style with attendants,
and bought the whole cargo on credit, leaving his signet ring with the ship’s captain.
28:
He had a tent put up nearby and told his attendants,
“When merchants come, announce them through three doorkeepers, one after another.”
29:
A hundred merchants from Bārāṇasī came for the cargo but heard it was bought on credit;
they went to the great merchant, announced through the three doorkeepers.
30:
Each merchant paid a thousand to become a partner, then another thousand to take over his share;
he gained two hundred thousand kahāpaṇas.
31:
In gratitude he took a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas to Cūḷaseṭṭhi. When asked how he got it,
he told how, starting from a dead mouse, he had made this wealth in four months.
32: Cūḷaseṭṭhi, not wanting to lose so wise a young man, gave him his daughter in marriage.
33: When Cūḷaseṭṭhi passed away, the young man took over the treasurer’s position in that city.
34:
The Buddha spoke the verse:
“As one fans a tiny spark into a fire, the wise rise up from small means.”
“The young man was Cūḷapanthaka, and Cūḷaseṭṭhi was I myself.”
